Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 70, verses 1–10:

Makkiyya (Meccan), and it contains one thousand one hundred and sixty letters, two hundred and sixteen words... 

Wait, I need to translate the text exactly as given. Here is the translation:

Meccan; it has one thousand one hundred and sixty letters, sixty-two words [sic: the text reads "اثنتان وست عشرة كلمة"], and forty-four verses.

Al-Tha'alibi reports: Muhammad ibn al-Qayyim told me, saying: Isma'il ibn Majid told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Sa'd told us, saying: Sa'd ibn Hafs told us, saying: I read to Ma'qil ibn Ubayd Allah, from Ikrimah ibn Khalid, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah Sa'ala sa'il, Allah will give him the reward of those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant, and who guard their prayers" [31] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/116.]].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that is to befall﴾. The people of Medina and Syria read sa'ala without hamza, while the rest read it with hamza, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this. Whoever reads it with hamza, it is from the question (su'al) only, and it has two aspects. One: the preposition "bi" in His words "bi-'adhabin" (with a punishment) is in the sense of "'an" (about), like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿fa-s'al bihi khabiran﴾ [[Surat al-Furqan: 59.]], meaning "about it." 'Alqama ibn 'Abda said:

"If you ask me about women, indeed I am
knowledgeable about the ailments of women, a physician."
[[Lisan al-'Arab: 1/554.]]

Meaning: about the women.

The meaning of the verse: a questioner asked about a punishment that is falling and descending: upon whom will it descend, and for whom is it? Then Allah, glorified is He, answered him: ﴿for the disbelievers﴾.

This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatada, who said: this was in Mecca, when Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to them and he warned them of punishment and retribution, and the polytheists said to one another: "Ask Muhammad about who will bear this punishment, upon whom it will descend and on whom it will fall." So Allah made it clear and sent down: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that is to befall, for the disbelievers﴾, i.e., upon the disbelievers; the lam is in the sense of "'ala" (upon). It refers to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, when he invoked against himself and asked for the punishment, saying: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth..." [[Qur'an 8:32.]] It befell him on the day of Badr, when he was killed in cold blood, and no other prisoner that day was killed except him and 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna was asked about whom this verse, "A questioner asked," was revealed concerning, and he said: "You have asked me about a matter that no one has asked me before you."

My father told me, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his forefathers, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at Ghadir Khumm, he called out to the people and they gathered; he took the hand of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: "Whoever I am his master, 'Ali is his master" [[Musnad Ahmad: 1/84, 5/347; al-Mustadrak: 3/110; Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba: 7/495.]].

This spread and was carried throughout the lands, and it reached al-Harith ibn al-Nu'man al-Fihri. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on his she-camel until he reached al-Abtah; he dismounted, made his camel kneel and tied it, then came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was among a group of his companions and said: "O Muhammad, you commanded us from Allah to testify that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah, and we accepted it from you. You commanded us to pray five times, and we accepted it from you. You commanded us to give zakat, and we accepted. You commanded us to perform Hajj, and we accepted. You commanded us to fast a month, and we accepted. Then you were not satisfied with this until you raised the arm of your cousin, preferred him over us, and said: 'Whoever I am his master, 'Ali is his master.' Is this a thing from you or from Allah, exalted is He?"

He said: "By Him other than whom there is no god, this is from Allah." Al-Harith ibn al-Nu'man turned away, heading for his mount, saying:

"O Allah, if what he says is true, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."

He had not reached his mount before Allah struck him with a stone that fell upon his head and came out through his back, killing him. And Allah, glorified is He, sent down: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that is to befall, for the disbelievers, which none can avert﴾ [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 18/279, at the verse.]].

Whoever reads without hamza has two aspects. One: it is a dialect form of the question; the Arabs say "sala sa'il" and "sa'ala sal," like "nala yanal" and "khafa yakhaf." The second: that it is from the flow (sayl). Zayd ibn Thabit and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "Sal" is a valley of Hell called "Sa'il."

﴿from Allah, Lord of the ascents﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means Lord of the heavens. Ibn Kaysan said: the ma'arij (ascents) is the cleft between two heavens and two earths. Qatada: Lord of the gradations and blessings. Sa'id ibn Jubayr: Lord of the degrees. Al-Qurtubi: Lord of the lofty virtues. Mujahid: the ascents of the angels.

﴿Ascend﴾ with the ya' is read by al-Kisa'i, and it is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and the preference of Abu 'Ubayd; others read it with the ta': ﴿the angels and the Spirit﴾, which is Jibril, ﴿ascend to Him﴾, to Allah, mighty and majestic, ﴿in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾, of the years of this world, which the angels alone would not ascend in; for they ascend from the furthest point of Allah's command, from beneath the seventh earth, to the furthest point of His command above the seventh heaven.

Al-Layth reported from Mujahid concerning ﴿in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾: from the furthest point of His command beneath the earths to the furthest point of His command above the heavens is the measure of fifty thousand years. And "a day whose measure is a thousand years" (32:5) refers to the descent of the command from the heaven to the earth and its ascent from the earth to the heaven in one day, which is the measure of a thousand years, because the distance between heaven and earth is a five-hundred-year journey.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar said: If the children of Adam were to travel from the world to the place of the Throne, they would travel for fifty thousand years before they crossed it.

al-Hakam ibn 'Ikrima said: it is the duration of the life of the world from its beginning to its end, fifty thousand years; none of you knows how much has passed and how much remains except Allah. Qatada said: it is the Day of Resurrection.

al-Hasan said: it is the Day of Resurrection, and it does not mean that its length is less than its duration; for if that were so, it would have an end, meaning the Garden and the Fire. Rather, it is the day of their standing for reckoning, until fifty thousand years of worldly years separate people. That is because the Day of Resurrection has a beginning and no end, for it is an extended day; if it had an end, it would be cut off.

It was also said: its meaning is that if anyone other than Allah were to take charge of the reckoning of the servants on that day, they would not finish it in fifty thousand years. This is the report of Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl from al-Kalbi, who said: "It is as if he said: if the angels, the jinn and mankind were to take charge of the reckoning of that day, and their reckoning lasted, they would not finish it in fifty thousand years, while I finish it in an hour of the day."

Yaman said: it is the Day of Resurrection, in which there are fifty stations, each station a thousand years, and there is inversion in the order, as if he said: ﴿none can avert it, from Allah ... in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years; the angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾.

Abu al-Jawza' and Ibn Abi Talha reported from Ibn 'Abbas: it is the Day of Resurrection, which Allah made, for the disbelievers, the measure of fifty thousand years, so that the people of the standing find that day long.

We were told by Ibn Fanjawayh, who said: al-Qati'i told us, who said: 'Abd Allah told us, who said: my father told us, who said: al-Hasan told us, who said: Ibn Lahi'a told us, who said: Darraj told us, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "A day whose measure is fifty thousand years, how long this day is!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, it will be made light for the believers until it is lighter for them than an obligatory prayer you pray in the world" [[Kashf al-Khafa': 2/385.]].

Ibrahim al-Taymi said: that day was no more for the believer than the span between noon and afternoon prayer.

﴿So be patient with patience, beautiful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they see it as distant﴾, meaning the punishment, ﴿but We see it as near﴾, because what is coming is near. ﴿On a day when the sky will be like molten brass﴾: like the dregs of oil; and it was said: like molten metal, and its explanation has passed. ﴿And the mountains will be like wool﴾: like dyed wool; "'ihn" is only said of dyed wool. Muqatil said: like carded wool. Al-Hasan said: like red wool, which is the weakest wool. The first change of the mountains is that they become a sand heap, then carded wool, then they become scattered dust.

﴿And no intimate friend will ask an intimate friend﴾: a close friend will not ask a close friend, due to being preoccupied with his own concern. And it was read ﴿wa-la yusalu﴾ with a ya' pronounced, i.e., no intimate friend will be asked about an intimate friend.

This spread and was carried throughout the lands, and it reached al-Harith ibn al-Nu'man al-Fihri. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on his she-camel until he reached al-Abtah; he dismounted, made his camel kneel and tied it, then came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was among a group of his companions and said: "O Muhammad, you commanded us from Allah to testify that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah, and we accepted it from you. You commanded us to pray five times, and we accepted it from you. You commanded us to give zakat, and we accepted. You commanded us to perform Hajj, and we accepted. You commanded us to fast a month, and we accepted. He said: "By Him other than whom there is no god, this is from Allah." Al-Harith ibn al-Nu'man turned away, heading for his mount, saying:

"O Allah, if what he says is true, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."

He had not reached his mount before Allah struck him with a stone that fell upon his head and came out through his back, killing him. Abu al-Jawza' and Ibn Abi Talha reported from Ibn 'Abbas: it is the Day of Resurrection, which Allah made, for the disbelievers, the measure of fifty thousand years, so that the people of the standing find that day long.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

﴿الَّذِينَ هُمْ عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ دائِمُونَ﴾.

Ibn Fanjawayh told us, who said: al-Qati'i told us, who said: Bishr ibn Musa told us, who said: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri' told us, from Hayawah, who said: Yazid ibn Abi Habib told me, from Abu al-Khayr Murthid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Yazani: that 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir said to them: "﴿الَّذِينَ هُمْ عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ دائِمُونَ﴾."

He said: We said: "Those who never cease praying?" He said: "No, rather those who, when they pray, do not turn their faces right or left."

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.
