**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 70, verses 11–35:**

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means "they see them" (yurawnahum). There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection, whether jinn or human, except that he is preoccupied with himself. A man sees his father, his brother, his kin and his clan, but does not ask about them. A man sees his close friend but does not speak to him, because they are all absorbed in themselves.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They recognize one another for a period of an hour of the day, and then after that they no longer recognize one another." Al-Suddi said: "﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ means they recognize them. As for the believer, it is by the whiteness of his face; as for the disbeliever, it is by the blackness of his face."

﴿يَوَدُّ الْمُجْرِمُ﴾ means the criminal, i.e. the polytheist, wishes (yatamanna). ﴿لَوْ يَفْتَدِي مِنْ عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ بِبَنِيهِ وَصاحِبَتِهِ﴾ means his wife, ﴿وَأَخِيهِ وَفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾ means his clan, the group from which he was separated. Abu 'Ubaydah said it means his subclan (fakhdh). Tha'lab said it means his nearest ancestors (aba'ihi al-adnin). Others said it means his closest relatives (aqribaihi al-aqrabin). ﴿الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ﴾ means the tribe that shelters him, according to Mujahid. ﴿وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعاً ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ means that this ransom would save him from the punishment of God, the Glorified. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means: no, it is not so; nothing will save him from the punishment of God.

Then He began, saying: ﴿إِنَّها لَظى﴾. It was said that the meaning is "truly, it is Laza" (haqqan), so that it is connected to what precedes. Laza is one of the names of Hell, and for this reason it is not declined (lam yujra). It was also said that it is the second level of Hell, named so because it blazes (tatalaz). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ [Surah al-Layl 92:14].

﴿نَزَّاعَةً﴾: the common reading is with a damma, as an attribute (na't) of Laza. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with a fatha, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) and as a detached qualifier (qata'). ﴿لِلشَّوى﴾: al-Kalbi said: it strips the head to eat the brain; then the brain returns as it was, and then it returns to eat it, and that is its perpetual state. This is also the narration of Abu Zabyan from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata', on his authority: it means the skins and the skull. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on his authority: it means the sinews and the heel-tendons. Mujahid said: it means the skin of the head. The evidence for this interpretation is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

*"Had the calamities struck you, they would have left the top of the head bare, its hair shaven."*

Ibrahim ibn Muhajir said: it means the flesh apart from the bone. The skull burns everything in it, and the heart remains intact. Abu Salih said: it means the flesh of the shin. Thabit al-Bunani said: it means the beauty of his face. Qatadah said: it means the nobility of his character and his limbs. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it means the attractive features of his face. Yaman said: it strips the limbs. Murrah said: it means the organs. Ibn Zayd said: it means the marrow of the bones. Al-Dahhak said: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone until it leaves nothing of it. Al-Kisa'i said: it means the joints. Ibn Jarir said: al-shawa is the plural of shawah, and it is among the parts of the human body which are not fatal; one says: "He shot and wounded (fa-ashwa)" when he did not hit a vital spot. Some of the scholars said: it means the limbs and the skins. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Lean of shin, thick of limb, tight of sinew."*

And al-A'sha said:

*"Qutaylah said: what has happened to him, that he has whitened the hair of his head?"*

﴿تَدْعُوا إلى نفسها﴾: it calls to itself those who turn away from faith (adbara 'an al-iman) ﴿وَتَوَلَّى﴾ from the truth, and says: "To me, to me!"

Ibn 'Abbas said: it calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in eloquent language, then it snatches them up as birds snatch up grain. Tha'lab said: ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾ means "destroys"; the Arabs say "God call you" (da'aka Allah), meaning God destroy you. Al-Khalil said: this is not calling in the sense of "come here"; rather, its calling them means its power over punishing them and its doing to them what it does.

﴿وَجَمَعَ الْمالَ فَأَوْعى﴾: he gathered wealth and kept it (amsaka), and did not pay God's due from it.

I was informed, and it is said that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Muhammad ibn Mansur told us, who said: Abu Fatn told us, who said: al-Mas'udi told us, from al-Hakam, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Hakim would not tie his purse, and he would say: "I heard God, the Glorified and Exalted, say: ﴿وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعى﴾."

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعاً﴾.

'Abd al-Khaliq told us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazdad al-Razi told us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Tahir al-Khath'ami told us, who said: Isma'il ibn Musa told us, who said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr told us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿هَلُوعاً﴾: he said: "the one greedy for what is not lawful to him."

'Ata' narrated from him: it is the one of whom God, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِذا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ جَزُوعاً وَإِذا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعاً﴾ [Surah al-Ma'arij 70:20–21]. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "stingy" (shahihan). 'Ikrimah said: "impatient" (dajuran). Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: "miserly" (bakhilan). Husayn said: "greedy" (haris). Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "anxious" (hazunan). Mujahid said: "rapacious" (sharrah). Also from al-Dahhak: al-halu'* is the one who is never satisfied. Muqatil said: "narrow of heart." Ibn Kaysan said: God created man loving what pleases him and gratifies him, and fleeing what he dislikes and what angers him; then He made him worship by spending what he loves and enjoys, and by patience in what he dislikes. 'Ata' said: "hasty." It was also said: "ignorant." Sahl said: "fickle in his desires and his whims." I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn 'Abd Allah say: I heard Abu al-Qayyim al-Bazzaz say: Ibn 'Ata' said: al-halu' is the one who is content with what is present and angry at what is absent. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: "he who forgets in times of blessing and supplicates in times of trial." Also from Sahl: when he is poor he is impatient, and when he is rich he withholds. Abu 'Ubaydah and Tha'lab said: it is the one who, when good touches him, does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, does not endure patiently. It was also said: it means "one who greatly desires," whom a little of the world satisfies and an equal amount angers. In the language, al-hal' means the most intense greed and the worst impatience.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The worst thing given to a servant is a miserly greed and a cowardly fear." [34] [Al-Fa'iq fi Gharib al-Hadith, 3:404.]

The Arabs say: "a camel that is hala'" (halwa') when it is swift in its pace and light. The poet said:

*"A camel, swift and light, when you turn your back on her; a lean, hard-striding one, when you face her, quick and light."*

Then God, the Glorified and Exalted, excepted: ﴿إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ﴾. It was said: they are the Companions specifically, and generally the believers, for they overcome excessive anxiety by the command of the Law, because of their trust in their Lord and their certainty of His power. He excepted the plural from the singular.

Because al-insan is a generic noun, it has the sense of the plural.

And His words: "What is wrong with them that they turn away from the Reminder?" (Surah al-Muddaththir 74:49).

*qibalaka muhti'in*: approaching (*muqbilin*), hastening (*musri'in*) toward you, raising their necks (*madddi a'naqahum*), with their gaze fixed on you (*mudimi al-nazar ilayk*), looking eagerly toward you (*mutala'inna nahwak*).

The explanation of *al-ihtta'* (hastening) has already passed. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*).

*'an al-yamini wa 'an al-shimali 'izin*: in circles (*halqan*) and in groups (*firaqan*), each faction (*'usbatan 'usbatan*) and each company (*jama'atan jama'atan*), scattered. *'Izin* means groups in dispersal, and its singular is *'izzah*. Its parallels in speech are *thubah* and *thubatin*, *kurah* and *kurin*, *qulah* and *qulin*. 'Antarah said:

*"And a troop I left to its own protector, over whom the birds hover like a notched sword, scattered."*

Al-Ra'i said:

*"O Caliph of the Merciful, my tribe has become like grazing herds scattered in groups, so were it not..."*

Another said:

*"As if the skulls, from the impact of its blows, were wild herds (khanatil) of scattered birds and beasts, dispersed in groups."*

Al-Tabari informed us, through 'Aqil, that al-Mu'afa reported to them from Ibn Jarir, who said: Bakkar related to us, saying: Mu'ammal related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah: The Prophet (ﷺ) went out to his companions while they were in circles, circle after circle, and said: "What is the matter with you that I see you in groups?"

The exegetes said: The polytheists used to gather around the Prophet (ﷺ) and listen to his words without benefiting from them. Rather, they denied him, lied about him, and mocked him and his companions, saying: "These people will enter Paradise as Muhammad says. So let us enter it before them, and let there be more in it for us than for them." Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed: *"Does every one of them aspire to enter a Garden of Bliss?"*

Al-Hasan and Talhah read it with a *fath* on the *ya'* and a *damm* on the *kha'* (*yudkhala*), and al-Mufaddal related the same from 'Asim. The rest read it in the opposite manner. *Kalla* ("No!"), they shall not enter it. Then he began: *"Indeed, We created them from that which they know."* That is, from a drop (*nutfah*), then a clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*). So none of them deserves Paradise by virtue of nobility, since the origin of creation is one. Rather, they deserve it through obedience. Qatadah said regarding this: "We created you, son of Adam, from filth, so fear Allah."

Ibn Fanjawayh informed us: Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Barzah related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Sulayman ibn al-Harith al-Baghandi related to us, saying: 'Arim Abu al-Nu'man al-Sadusi related to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah related to us from Thabit, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, whenever he addressed us, mentioned the stench of the children of Adam. He described their origin: that one emerges from the place of urine twice, then falls into the womb as a drop, then a clot, then a lump, then comes out from his mother's belly, and then he is soiled with his urine and excrement until one of us becomes disgusted with himself.

Ibn Fanjawayh also informed me, saying: Musa ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali related to us, saying: Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Firyabi related to us, saying: Safwan ibn Salih related to us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim related to us, saying: Jarir ibn 'Uthman related to us from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Maysarah, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Bisr ibn Jahhash, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and one day he spat into his palm and placed his finger upon it: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Son of Adam, how can you escape Me when I created you from the likes of this? Until, when I had perfected you and made you balanced, you walked between two cloaks, and the earth was gentle upon you. That is, for the sake of the family of Layla.

It has also been said that *ma* here means *man* (those who), and the sense is: "We created them from among those who know and understand, not like the beasts."

*Yawma yakhruju*: the common reading is with a *fath* on the *ya'* and a *damm* on the *ra'*. Al-A'sha reported from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, a *damm* on the *ya'* and a *fath* on the *ra'* (*yukhraju*). *Min al-ajdath*: from the graves (*al-qubur*). *Sira'an*: hastening toward responding to the caller. *Ka'annahum ila nasbin*: the common reading is with a *fath* on the *nun* and a *jazm* on the *sad* (*nasb*), meaning "toward something set up," as one says: "So-and-so is set before my eyes."

*"Knights of Dhubyan under the iron, like jinn rushing out from 'Abqar."*

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: they run. Abu al-'Aliyah and Mujahid said: they race one another. Al-Dahhak said: they rise up. Al-Hasan said: they hurry. Al-Qurazi said: they press forward.

*Khashi'atan*: humbled, abased. *Absaruhum*: their gazes [are fixed] on the punishment. Qatadah said: "The darkness of their faces." *Tarhaquhum dhillah*: humiliation covers them, disgrace overtakes them. From this comes the term *muraahiq* for a youth who has reached the age of puberty when the wet dream has overtaken him.

*Dhalika al-yawm alladhi kanu yu'adun*: this is the Day of Resurrection.

And His words: "What is wrong with them that they turn away from the Reminder?" (Surah al-Muddaththir 74:49).

*qibalaka muhti'in*: approaching (*muqbilin*), hastening (*musri'in*) toward you, raising their necks (*madddi a'naqahum*), with their gaze fixed on you (*mudimi al-nazar ilayk*), looking eagerly toward you (*mutala'inna nahwak*).

The explanation of *al-ihtta'* (hastening) has already passed. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*).

Its parallels in speech are *thubah* and *thubatin*, *kurah* and *kurin*, *qulah* and *qulin*. 'Antarah said:

*"And a troop I left to its own protector, over whom the birds hover like a notched sword, scattered."*

Al-Ra'i said:

*"O Caliph of the Merciful, my tribe has become like grazing herds scattered in groups, so were it not..."*

Another said:

*"As if the skulls, from the impact of its blows, were wild herds (khanatil) of scattered birds and beasts, dispersed in groups."*

Al-Tabari informed us, through 'Aqil, that al-Mu'afa reported to them from Ibn Jarir, who said: Bakkar related to us, saying: Mu'ammal related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah: The Prophet (ﷺ) went out to his companions while they were in circles, circle after circle, and said: "What is the matter with you that I see you in groups?"

The exegetes said: The polytheists used to gather around the Prophet (ﷺ) and listen to his words without benefiting from them. Rather, they denied him, lied about him, and mocked him and his companions, saying: "These people will enter Paradise as Muhammad says. So let us enter it before them, and let there be more in it for us than for them." Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed: *"Does every one of them aspire to enter a Garden of Bliss?"*

Al-Hasan and Talhah read it with a *fath* on the *ya'* and a *damm* on the *kha'* (*yudkhala*), and al-Mufaddal related the same from 'Asim. The rest read it in the opposite manner. *Kalla* ("No!"), they shall not enter it. Then he began: *"Indeed, We created them from that which they know."* That is, from a drop (*nutfah*), then a clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*). So none of them deserves Paradise by virtue of nobility, since the origin of creation is one. Rather, they deserve it through obedience. Qatadah said regarding this: "We created you, son of Adam, from filth, so fear Allah."

Ibn Fanjawayh informed us: Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Barzah related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Sulayman ibn al-Harith al-Baghandi related to us, saying: 'Arim Abu al-Nu'man al-Sadusi related to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah related to us from Thabit, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, whenever he addressed us, mentioned the stench of the children of Adam. He described their origin: that one emerges from the place of urine twice, then falls into the womb as a drop, then a clot, then a lump, then comes out from his mother's belly, and then he is soiled with his urine and excrement until one of us becomes disgusted with himself.

Ibn Fanjawayh also informed me, saying: Musa ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali related to us, saying: Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Firyabi related to us, saying: Safwan ibn Salih related to us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim related to us, saying: Jarir ibn 'Uthman related to us from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Maysarah, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Bisr ibn Jahhash, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and one day he spat into his palm and placed his finger upon it: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Son of Adam, how can you escape Me when I created you from the likes of this? Until, when I had perfected you and made you balanced, you walked between two cloaks, and the earth was gentle upon you. Then you gathered and withheld, until when the collarbones (*taraqi*) reached, you said: "I will give charity," and when is the time for charity?'"

That is, for the sake of the family of Layla.

It has also been said that *ma* here means *man* (those who), and the sense is: "We created them from among those who know and understand, not like the beasts."

*Yawma yakhruju*: the common reading is with a *fath* on the *ya'* and a *damm* on the *ra'*. Al-A'sha reported from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, a *damm* on the *ya'* and a *fath* on the *ra'* (*yukhraju*). *Min al-ajdath*: from the graves (*al-qubur*). *Sira'an*: hastening toward responding to the caller. *Ka'annahum ila nasbin*: the common reading is with a *fath* on the *nun* and a *jazm* on the *sad* (*nasb*), meaning "toward something set up," as one says: "So-and-so is set before my eyes."

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means "toward a goal," and that is when they hear the final Blast. Al-Kalbi said: "toward a sign and a standard." Abu al-'Ala' said: I heard some Arabs say: *al-nusb* is the snare into which the game falls, and its owner hastens to it lest the game escape from it. *"Knights of Dhubyan under the iron, like jinn rushing out from 'Abqar."*

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: they run. Abu al-'Aliyah and Mujahid said: they race one another. Al-Dahhak said: they rise up. Al-Hasan said: they hurry. Al-Qurazi said: they press forward.

*Khashi'atan*: humbled, abased. *Absaruhum*: their gazes [are fixed] on the punishment. Qatadah said: "The darkness of their faces." *Tarhaquhum dhillah*: humiliation covers them, disgrace overtakes them. From this comes the term *muraahiq* for a youth who has reached the age of puberty when the wet dream has overtaken him.

*Dhalika al-yawm alladhi kanu yu'adun*: this is the Day of Resurrection.
